before.content_html:
The 1920s Economic Boom

In the 1920s, the USA saw rapid economic growth known as the ‘Boom.’ Mass production, hire purchase, and new advertising fuelled a consumer society that changed American life. The decade became the ‘Roaring Twenties’ as many Americans enjoyed new prosperity and optimism.

Why Did the US Economy Boom?

Republican Government Policies

The Republican presidents — Warren Harding (1921–1923), Calvin Coolidge (1923–1929), and Herbert Hoover (1929–1933) — believed in laissez-faire: the government should stay out of the economy. They kept taxes low and introduced tariffs (taxes on imported goods) to protect American businesses. The Fordney-McCumber Tariff of 1922 raised import duties to their highest levels, making foreign goods more expensive and pushing Americans to buy home-produced products.

New Industries and Mass Production

New consumer goods — cars, radios, refrigerators, vacuum cleaners, washing machines — were produced on a huge scale. New materials like plastics made it cheaper to manufacture everyday items, from combs and buttons to radio casings. Henry Ford pioneered the assembly line at his Detroit factories. His Model T car — nicknamed the ‘Tin Lizzie’ — took 12 hours to build in 1913 but just 93 minutes by the mid-1920s. The key was standardisation: every Model T was identical, with only one colour (black) and one engine size. As Ford famously said, “A customer can have any colour he likes so long as it’s black.” Standardised parts meant fewer skilled workers were needed, cutting wage costs dramatically. The price fell from $1,200 in 1909 to just $295 by 1928, making it affordable for ordinary families. By 1929, Ford was producing more than one car every three minutes.

Key Fact — Henry Ford

Ford’s assembly line transformed American manufacturing. He paid workers $5 a day — double the average wage — and introduced the five-day working week, which was revolutionary at the time. He also paid Black workers the same as white workers. Well-paid workers becoming consumers helped drive the wider boom. However, Ford refused to allow trade unions, the hours were long with few breaks, and he used intimidation against workers who complained. At his vast Rouge River plant, 81,000 men worked in a single factory by 1929.

The Motor Car Industry

The car industry had a huge knock-on effect on the economy — often called the ‘Cycle of Prosperity.’ Car production consumed 20% of America’s steel, 80% of its rubber, 75% of its plate glass, and 65% of its leather. By the end of the 1920s, American cars were using seven billion gallons of petrol a year, making oil-producing states like Texas wealthy. New roads, highways, petrol stations, motels, and roadside restaurants sprang up, creating thousands more jobs. Suburbs grew as people drove to work. By 1929, motor manufacturing was America’s biggest industry, employing hundreds of thousands directly and millions more in related trades. In Europe, cars were still a luxury for the rich — in America, they were becoming an everyday item.

Hire Purchase

Americans could now buy expensive goods on credit — known as hire purchase or ‘buying on the instalment plan.’ They paid a small deposit, then monthly payments. By 1929, 60% of cars and 80% of radios were bought this way. Easy credit boosted spending and demand.

Advertising

New advertising on radio, billboards, newspapers, and magazines pushed Americans to buy the latest products. Advertisers created a culture of consumerism, making people feel they needed the newest goods to keep up with their neighbours. Mail-order catalogues brought consumer goods to rural families who lived far from shops, spreading the boom beyond the cities. By 1929, over 10 million radios sat in American homes.

The Stock Market

Many Americans bought shares (stocks) in companies, hoping for quick profits as prices rose. This was called speculation. Some bought ‘on the margin’ — borrowing money to invest. The rising stock market created a sense of confidence, and millions believed the boom would last forever.

Natural Resources and WWI

The USA had vast natural resources — oil, coal, and iron — which fuelled industrial growth. During World War One, the USA lent money to European countries and sold them weapons and supplies. After the war, European economies were weak, letting America dominate world trade. The USA had also taken over markets that Europe used to supply.

Who Benefited from the Boom?

The boom did not help everyone equally. Winners included:

  • Businessmen and industrialists — factory and company owners saw profits soar.
  • Workers in new industries like cars, electrical goods, and construction — higher wages and better living standards.
  • City dwellers — access to new consumer goods, entertainment, and jobs.
  • Stock market speculators — profits as share prices kept rising.
  • Middle-class families — could afford cars, radios, and refrigerators on hire purchase.

Who Did NOT Benefit?

Many Americans were left behind. The prosperity of the ‘Roaring Twenties’ was very uneven:

Farmers: Overproduction meant crop prices collapsed. During WWI, farmers had expanded to feed Europe, but after the war demand fell. Around 600,000 farmers lost their farms, and farm income dropped from $22 billion (1919) to $13 billion (1928).

African Americans: Most lived in the South as sharecroppers, trapped in poverty and debt. They faced Jim Crow segregation and violence from the Ku Klux Klan. Even in northern cities, they got the lowest-paid, most dangerous jobs and lived in overcrowded ghettos.

Native Americans: The poorest group in 1920s America. They lived on reservations with limited education, healthcare, and jobs. Life expectancy was far lower than for white Americans.

Workers in old industries: Coal, textiles, and leather struggled against new materials and technologies. Coal demand fell as oil and electricity grew. Textile workers saw wages cut as factories moved south for cheaper labour.

Recent immigrants: Many worked low-paid, dangerous jobs and faced hostility. Immigration laws in 1921 and 1924 severely restricted who could enter the country.

Key Fact — Hidden Poverty

Despite the image of prosperity, around 42% of Americans lived below the poverty line in 1929. The richest 5% received about 33% of all income. Millions could not afford the consumer goods being produced — a weakness that would help cause the crash.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following had more impact on the American economy in the 1920s:

• mass production and new technology
• Republican government policies?

Explain your answer with reference to both bullet points.
practice_questions.marks:
All relevant and accurate points should be credited.
Top band (10-12): Complex explanation of both bullets leading to a sustained judgement. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate and detailed knowledge and understanding. Students explain the relationship between causes arriving at a sustained judgement.
Example: Both factors were crucial and reinforced each other. Mass production was arguably more directly important: Ford’s assembly line cut the Model T build time from 12 hours to 93 minutes and the price from $1,200 to $295, creating a consumer revolution. The car industry consumed 20% of America’s steel and 80% of its rubber, with knock-on effects across the economy. However, Republican policies created the conditions for this growth. Laissez-faire meant low taxes, leaving businesses with more capital to invest in new technology. The Fordney-McCumber Tariff of 1922 protected American manufacturers from foreign competition. Without these policies, mass production might not have been as profitable. Ultimately, mass production had the greater direct impact on everyday Americans’ lives, but Republican policies provided the framework that allowed it to flourish.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Developed explanation of both bullets. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate knowledge and understanding. Extended reasoning supported by developed factual knowledge.
Example (bullet 1): Mass production transformed the economy. Ford’s assembly line made goods affordable — the Model T fell to $295 by 1928. New consumer goods like radios and fridges were mass-produced, and by 1929 over 10 million radios were in American homes.
Example (bullet 2): Republican policies also helped. Presidents Harding, Coolidge, and Hoover kept taxes low and the Fordney-McCumber Tariff protected American businesses from cheaper foreign imports.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Simple explanation of bullet(s). Answer demonstrates specific knowledge and understanding. Simple reasoning supported by factual knowledge.
Example: Mass production made goods cheaper. Ford’s cars became affordable for ordinary families.
Lower band (1-3): Basic explanation of bullet(s). Basic knowledge, explanation likely implicit or by assertion.

before.exam_tip_html: This lesson covers two AQA spec points: entertainment (cinema, jazz) and the position of women (flappers). For top marks, show how they connect — flappers were part of the new entertainment culture, and cinema spread new ideas about women nationwide. Always discuss both change and its limits: who experienced the new culture, and who was excluded by geography, race, or class?
before.content_html:
A Cultural Revolution

The 1920s were not just an economic boom — they were a cultural revolution. Cinema, jazz, radio, and spectator sports created a shared national culture for the first time. Changing attitudes gave women new freedoms. These shifts earned the decade its famous nickname: the ‘Roaring Twenties.’

The Growth of Cinema

Cinema became the most popular form of entertainment in 1920s America. By the end of the decade, about 100 million Americans — out of a population of 123 million — went to the cinema every week. Almost every person in the country was visiting a movie theatre weekly.

Hollywood and the Studio System

Hollywood, in Los Angeles, became the centre of the American film industry. Major studios like Paramount, MGM, Warner Bros., and Universal turned out around 500 films a year by 1929. The sunny Californian climate was ideal for filming, and the studios built vast lots to make movies on an almost industrial scale.

Most of the decade was the era of silent films. Stars like Charlie Chaplin, Buster Keaton, Mary Pickford, and Rudolph Valentino became household names. Clara Bow, known as the ‘It Girl,’ became the flapper icon on screen — her image of fun, freedom, and sex appeal defined 1920s glamour. Audiences did not need to understand English to enjoy silent films, making cinema a truly universal form of entertainment.

Key Fact — The Jazz Singer (1927)

In October 1927, Warner Bros. released The Jazz Singer, the first major film with synchronised dialogue — a ‘talkie.’ Starring Al Jolson, it was a sensation. It ended the silent era and launched modern cinema. Within two years, virtually all films were ‘talkies.’

The Impact of Cinema on American Culture

Cinema shaped how Americans thought and behaved. Films spread new fashions, hairstyles, and attitudes across the country. A woman in small-town Kansas could see the same film as a woman in New York and copy the same style. Cinema helped create a shared national culture, breaking down rural isolation.

Movie stars became celebrities on a scale never seen before. Fans copied their clothes, hair, and mannerisms. Cinema also promoted consumerism — audiences saw characters using the latest products and wanted them. However, not everyone approved. The Hays Code set moral guidelines for films — no kiss longer than 3 seconds, no nudity, and clergy could not be shown as villains. The Code showed the tension between modern culture and traditional values.

Jazz and the Jazz Age

Jazz music was the soundtrack of the 1920s — energetic, improvisational, and exciting. The decade became known as the ‘Jazz Age,’ a term coined by the writer F. Scott Fitzgerald.

Origins in African American Communities

Jazz grew out of African American musical traditions in the South, especially New Orleans. It blended blues, ragtime, and spirituals — music rooted in the experience of slavery, hardship, and resilience.

During the Great Migration, hundreds of thousands of African Americans moved from the rural South to northern cities. They brought jazz with them. Chicago, New York, and Kansas City became major jazz centres, with clubs playing the new music night after night.

Key Jazz Figures

Key Fact — Louis Armstrong

Louis Armstrong was the most important jazz musician of the 1920s. Born in New Orleans, he moved to Chicago and became famous for his trumpet playing and warm, gravelly voice. Armstrong proved jazz was a serious art form, not just dance music. He was one of the first African American entertainers to win a large white audience.

Other key figures included Duke Ellington, whose orchestra performed at the famous Cotton Club in Harlem, and Bessie Smith, the ‘Empress of the Blues,’ one of the highest-paid Black performers in America. Josephine Baker became a major Jazz Age entertainer, famous for her daring dance performances — though she found greater acceptance in Paris than in segregated America. White musicians like Bix Beiderbecke also played jazz, showing the music was crossing racial lines.

Jazz and Controversy

Not everyone welcomed jazz. Older, conservative Americans — especially in rural areas and the South — saw it as immoral, dangerous, and corrupting. They linked it to drinking, dancing, and racial mixing. Some called it ‘the devil’s music.’ This clash between modern, urban culture and traditional, rural values was one of the defining conflicts of the 1920s.

The Harlem Renaissance

Jazz was part of a wider flowering of African American art, literature, and culture called the Harlem Renaissance. Harlem, in New York City, became the centre of Black cultural life in America.

Writers like Langston Hughes and Zora Neale Hurston explored the African American experience in poetry and novels. Artists, musicians, and intellectuals built a powerful sense of Black pride and identity. The Harlem Renaissance challenged racist stereotypes and showed African Americans making vital contributions to American culture — even as they still faced severe discrimination.

Radio: A New Mass Medium

The radio transformed entertainment and culture. The first commercial station, KDKA in Pittsburgh, began broadcasting in November 1920. By 1929, over 10 million radios sat in American homes.

Key Fact — Radio’s Reach

Radio brought music, news, comedy, drama, and sports into people’s homes for the first time. Families gathered around the radio each evening. By 1929, the National Broadcasting Company (NBC) was reaching a nationwide audience, helping create a shared American culture across regional and class lines.

Radio also drove advertising and consumerism. Companies sponsored programmes, and adverts reached millions. Radio helped jazz spread far beyond the cities — a farmer in Iowa could now hear the same music as a city-dweller in Chicago.

Spectator Sports

The 1920s were a golden age of American sport. Rising incomes, more leisure time, and the growth of radio turned sport into mass entertainment.

Baseball was America’s favourite sport. Babe Ruth, playing for the New York Yankees, hit a record 60 home runs in 1927. He earned $80,000 a year — more than the President. Ruth was one of the first true sporting celebrities.

Boxing was the other great spectator sport. Jack Dempsey, the heavyweight champion, drew huge crowds. His 1921 fight against Georges Carpentier was the first event to earn over $1 million in ticket sales. About 300,000 people listened on radio — one of the first live sports broadcasts.

These sporting heroes became symbols of a confident, modern America. Sport, like cinema and jazz, built a sense of national identity and shared experience.

A New, Modern Society

Cinema, jazz, radio, and sport together marked a huge shift in American society. For the first time, people across the country shared the same entertainment, music, and heroes. Urban, modern values spread outward from the cities, clashing with the more traditional, religious values of rural America. This tension — between the old America and the new — is a key theme for the exam.

Women Before the 1920s

Before World War One, most American women’s lives centred on the home. Middle-class women were expected to be wives and mothers, dress modestly, and avoid public life. Women could not vote in federal elections, had limited access to education, and very few held professional jobs.

The Impact of World War One

The war changed things fast. With millions of men away fighting, women filled jobs in factories, offices, and farms. By 1918, around 1 million women had entered new roles. This gave many women independence and confidence, and it became harder to argue they were incapable of working or taking part in public life.

The 19th Amendment: Women’s Suffrage

The 19th Amendment was ratified on 18 August 1920, granting women the right to vote in all elections. It capped decades of campaigning by activists like Susan B. Anthony, Elizabeth Cady Stanton, and Alice Paul.

Key Fact — The 19th Amendment

The 19th Amendment stated: ‘The right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of sex.’ In practice, many African American women (and men) in the South were still blocked from voting by poll taxes, literacy tests, and intimidation.

The Flappers

The most visible symbol of changing women’s roles was the flapper. Flappers were young, fashionable women — mainly white, middle-class, and urban — who deliberately broke the rules about how women should look and behave. They were tied to the new jazz culture: dancing in nightclubs and speakeasies, part of the same modern world as cinema and radio.

How Did Flappers Challenge Convention?

  • Fashion: Flappers wore short skirts (knee-length — scandalous at the time), bobbed their hair, and used make-up in public. They rejected the modest clothing of previous generations.
  • Behaviour: They smoked in public, drank at speakeasies, danced to jazz, and drove cars. They went out without chaperones and socialised freely with men.
  • Attitudes: Flappers rejected the idea that a woman’s only role was wife and mother. They embraced fun, leisure, and personal choice.
Key Fact — Jazz and the Flappers

Jazz music became the soundtrack of the flapper lifestyle. Dances like the Charleston and the Black Bottom shocked older generations. Flappers flocked to dance halls and jazz clubs, making the music central to 1920s youth culture.

Wider Changes for Women

Changes in women’s lives went beyond the flapper image:

Employment

Women in employment rose by 25% during the 1920s, reaching about 10.6 million by 1929. Office work created new roles — secretaries, typists, telephone operators, shop assistants. But women were still paid less than men, and most professional careers stayed closed to them.

New Technology in the Home

Vacuum cleaners, washing machines, and refrigerators cut the time women spent on housework, freeing time for leisure, education, or paid work. But these devices were expensive and only wealthier families could afford them.

Birth Control

Margaret Sanger campaigned for women’s access to birth control. She opened the first birth control clinic in 1916 and founded the American Birth Control League in 1921. Contraception gave some women greater control over family size, though it stayed controversial and many states restricted access.

Education

By 1928, there were 10 times as many female college students as in 1900. Education opened new career paths and gave women greater economic independence.

Limits of Change

Do not overstate the changes. The flapper lifestyle was experienced by only a small minority of women:

Rural vs Urban: The flapper trend was mainly urban and middle-class. In rural areas, traditional values dominated. Only about 1 in 4 women worked outside the home.

Race: African American, Hispanic, and immigrant women saw far fewer benefits. Most were confined to low-paid domestic or farm work. African American women in the South faced both racial segregation and gender inequality.

Class: The flapper lifestyle needed money. Working-class women could not afford fashionable clothes, dance halls, or new goods. Many worked long hours for low pay.

Political impact: Despite the vote, women did not vote as a bloc. Very few were elected to office. The political establishment stayed overwhelmingly male.

Backlash: Many Americans — especially in rural, religious communities — opposed the changes. Religious leaders condemned flapper behaviour as sinful. Some states even tried to restrict hemline lengths by law. Even some younger women pushed back — the Anti-Flirt Club, founded in Washington D.C. in 1923, campaigned against the bold behaviour associated with flappers.

Introduction: A Nation of Divisions

The ‘Roaring Twenties’ hid deep divisions. While some enjoyed new wealth and freedoms, millions faced racism, prejudice, and poverty. Around 60% of American families lived below the poverty line — even during the boom. Tensions between old and new, native-born and immigrant, white and Black, rich and poor ran through every part of society.

This lesson covers economic inequality, the causes of racial tension, the experiences of immigrants, the revival of the Ku Klux Klan, and the Red Scare — including the case of Sacco and Vanzetti.

Economic Inequality Beneath the Boom

Not everyone shared in 1920s prosperity. The boom was largely an urban, industrial success story. Millions in rural America and in older industries were left behind.

Farmers in Crisis

American farmers had expanded production during World War One to feed Europe. After the war, demand dropped and prices collapsed. Around 6 million farmers were forced off their land during the 1920s. Mechanisation — especially combine harvesters and tractors — replaced manual labour, cutting the number of jobs available in farming.

Declining Industries

Workers in older industries also suffered. Coal miners faced low wages and dangerous conditions as oil and electricity replaced coal. Textile workers in New England saw jobs move south, where wages were lower. These workers had no share in the consumer boom happening in cities.

The Rural–Urban Divide

A deep cultural divide separated rural and urban America. Cities were centres of jazz, cinema, new fashions, and liberal attitudes. Rural America — especially in the South and Midwest — was more traditionalist, religious, and conservative. Many rural Americans saw city life as immoral and un-American. This clash fuelled support for Prohibition, hostility to immigration, and the revival of the KKK.

Key Fact — Poverty in the Boom

Around 60% of American families earned less than $2,000 per year — the minimum needed for a decent standard of living. About 6 million farmers lost their land. The boom mainly benefited white, urban, middle-class Americans, not the majority of the population.

The Causes of Racial Tension

Racial tension in 1920s America had deep roots. The country had a long history of discrimination against non-white groups, and the 1920s saw these tensions grow worse.

The Great Migration

During and after World War One, hundreds of thousands of African Americans moved from the rural South to northern cities. This movement was called the Great Migration. They were escaping sharecropping poverty, lynching violence, and the humiliation of Jim Crow laws.

By 1920, there were around 11 million Black Americans living in the USA. In cities like Chicago, Detroit, and New York, African Americans hoped for better factory jobs. They still faced serious discrimination — given the lowest-paid and most dangerous jobs, forced into overcrowded ghettos, and resented by white workers who saw them as competition.

Key Fact — The Great Migration

Between 1916 and 1930, about 1.5 million African Americans left the South for northern cities. They still faced prejudice. In 1919, race riots broke out in over 25 cities during the ‘Red Summer.’ The worst was in Chicago, where 38 people were killed.

Jim Crow and Segregation

In the Southern states, African Americans lived under Jim Crow laws — legal racial segregation. These laws kept Black and white people apart in schools, restaurants, buses, parks, and hospitals. Black people were denied the vote through literacy tests, poll taxes, and the ‘grandfather clause’ (you could only vote if your grandfather had voted — impossible for descendants of enslaved people).

Segregation was backed up by violence. Lynching — the murder of Black people by white mobs — was common. Between 1882 and 1968, nearly 5,000 lynchings were recorded, mostly of African Americans in the South. The federal government repeatedly failed to pass anti-lynching laws.

Immigration and Its Impact

The USA had long been a nation of immigrants. By the 1920s, attitudes had turned sharply against newcomers — especially those from Southern and Eastern Europe.

Who Were the Immigrants?

Between 1850 and 1914, around 40 million people emigrated to the USA. The earliest settlers — the ‘old immigrants’ — came mainly from Britain, Germany, Holland, and Scandinavia. Their descendants held the best jobs, the most wealth, and most political power. They were the WASPs (White Anglo-Saxon Protestants). America was described as a ‘melting pot’ — the idea being that all races would mix together and become one nation.

From the late nineteenth century, ‘new immigrants’ arrived from Italy, Poland, Russia, Greece, and the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Many were Catholic or Jewish, spoke little English, and had very different cultures from the WASPs. A smaller number of Hispanics and Asians also arrived. These new immigrants settled in cities, living in ethnic neighbourhoods and working in factories, mines, and construction.

Why Did Attitudes Harden?

Hostility towards immigrants grew for several reasons:

  • Competition for jobs: Native-born Americans resented immigrants who worked for lower wages.
  • Cultural fears: Immigrants brought different languages, religions, and customs. Many WASPs feared America’s identity was being diluted.
  • The Red Scare: After the Russian Revolution of 1917, many feared immigrants from Eastern Europe were bringing communist and anarchist ideas.
  • Racism: Pseudo-scientific ideas about racial superiority were widespread. Many Americans saw Southern and Eastern Europeans as racially inferior.

Immigration Restriction

Growing hostility led to new laws that slashed immigration:

1917

Immigration Act

Introduced a literacy test — immigrants had to prove they could read and write. This targeted poorer immigrants from Southern and Eastern Europe.

1921

Emergency Quota Act

Set a maximum of 375,000 immigrants per year. Each country was limited to 3% of the number from that country already in the USA (based on the 1910 census). This was the first numerical cap on immigration.

1924

National Origins Act (Johnson-Reed Act)

Tightened quotas to 2% of each nationality, now based on the 1890 census — before the surge of Southern and Eastern European immigration. This deliberately favoured Northern and Western Europeans and blocked Italians, Poles, Russians, and Greeks.

1929

Immigration Act

Total immigration was capped at just 150,000 per year. Immigration from Asia was banned entirely. This completed a decade of increasingly restrictive controls.

The Ku Klux Klan

The Ku Klux Klan (KKK) was a white supremacist group that first appeared after the Civil War in the 1860s. It was revived in 1915 and grew rapidly during the 1920s.

The Revival of the Klan

The KKK was re-founded in 1915 by William J. Simmons at Stone Mountain, Georgia, inspired by the hit film The Birth of a Nation (1915). The new Klan kept the old symbols — white robes, hoods, burning crosses — but expanded its targets to include Catholics, Jews, immigrants, and anyone seen as ‘un-American.’

Growth and Membership

Under Hiram Wesley Evans, who became Imperial Wizard in 1922, the Klan grew fast. It used professional recruiters called ‘Kleagles’ and charged $10 to join (a large sum then), with the recruiter keeping $4. Its message of white, Protestant, native-born supremacy appealed to those who felt threatened by change.

Key Fact — KKK Membership

At its peak, the Klan had 4–5 million members. It was not just a Southern movement — states like Indiana, Ohio, Oregon, and Oklahoma had huge memberships. In Indiana, about 30% of all white men were members. Klan-backed candidates won governorships and seats in Congress.

Klan Methods and Violence

The KKK used intimidation, beatings, tarring and feathering, arson, and murder. It boycotted Black-owned and Jewish-owned businesses. In 1925, 40,000 Klansmen marched down Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington, D.C. The Klan claimed to defend traditional American values and the Protestant faith.

The Klan collapsed in the late 1920s, mainly because of the D.C. Stephenson scandal. Stephenson, the Grand Dragon of the Indiana Klan, was convicted in 1925 of the kidnap, rape, and murder of Madge Oberholtzer. This exposed the Klan’s hypocrisy.

From prison, Stephenson named politicians who had taken Klan bribes. Several were jailed. Membership fell from millions to about 30,000 by 1930. The Klan did not vanish entirely — it resurfaced during the Civil Rights movement of the 1950s–60s.

The Red Scare

After World War One and the Russian Revolution of 1917, fear swept across America. Many were terrified that communists and anarchists were plotting to overthrow the government. This panic became the Red Scare.

Why Were Americans Afraid?

Key events fuelled the panic:

  • The Russian Revolution (1917) overthrew the Russian government and set up a communist state. Many feared the same in America.
  • In 1919, a wave of strikes hit the USA, including a general strike in Seattle and a police strike in Boston. Many Americans blamed communists.
  • In April and June 1919, anarchists sent bombs to politicians and businessmen, including Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer. One bomb damaged his home.

The Palmer Raids

Attorney General Palmer launched raids against suspected radicals. Between November 1919 and January 1920, his agents arrested over 6,000 people. Many were held without charge and denied lawyers. Around 500 foreign-born suspects were deported, including anarchist Emma Goldman.

The raids were popular at first, but support faded when Palmer clearly exaggerated the threat. His prediction of a communist revolution on 1 May 1920 never happened, and he was ridiculed. The Red Scare calmed down, but suspicion of immigrants and radicals lasted throughout the decade.

The Sacco and Vanzetti Case

The most famous example of how the Red Scare and anti-immigrant prejudice combined was the case of Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti.

The Crime

In April 1920, paymaster Fred Parmenter and an armed guard were shot dead during a robbery at a shoe factory in South Braintree, Massachusetts. About $15,000 was stolen. Before he died, Parmenter described his attackers as “slim foreigners with olive skins.” Three weeks later, Sacco (a shoe-maker) and Vanzetti (a fish-seller) were arrested. Both were Italian immigrants and anarchists who had dodged the military draft.

The Trial

Their 1921 trial was deeply controversial. The evidence was weak. The judge, Webster Thayer, was openly hostile — he reportedly called them “those anarchist bastards” outside court. Both were found guilty of murder and sentenced to death.

Many believed they were convicted for being Italian, immigrant, and anarchist — not because of the evidence. The case became a worldwide cause, with protests across Europe and South America.

Over six years, their lawyers launched appeals. A convicted criminal named Celestino Madeiros confessed to the robbery and said Sacco and Vanzetti were innocent. All appeals were rejected — several by the same Judge Thayer.

A special committee reviewed the case in 1927 but upheld the verdict. On 23 August 1927, Sacco and Vanzetti were executed by electric chair. Their deaths sparked worldwide protests. In 1977, the Governor of Massachusetts declared the trial unfair.

The Significance of the Case

The case exposed deep prejudice against immigrants and radicals. It showed how the Red Scare and anti-immigrant feeling could corrupt the justice system. It became a symbol of the intolerance beneath the surface of the ‘Roaring Twenties.’
before.conclusion_html:
Conclusion

The 1920s were deeply divided. Around 60% of families lived below the poverty line, 6 million farmers lost their land, and rural America clashed culturally with the cities. African Americans faced racism and violence North and South. Immigrants were shut out by quota laws. The KKK had millions of members. Sacco and Vanzetti’s execution showed how fear and prejudice could corrupt justice. The ‘Roaring Twenties’ was no golden age for most Americans.

Key Takeaways

  • Economic division: 60% of families lived below the poverty line. 6 million farmers were forced off their land by falling prices and mechanisation.
  • Racial tension and the KKK: The Great Migration, Jim Crow, and the KKK (4–5 million members) showed that racism shaped every part of American life.
  • Immigration restriction: The 1921 and 1924 quota laws cut immigration from 800,000 to 150,000 a year, deliberately targeting Southern and Eastern Europeans.

before.conclusion_html:
Conclusion

The Wall Street Crash was not just a stock market event. Years of speculation, overproduction, hire purchase debt, unequal wealth, and an unregulated banking system had built an economy on borrowed money and false confidence. Republican laissez-faire meant nobody stepped in to control the risks. When panic hit in October 1929, the whole structure collapsed, dragging millions into poverty and launching the Great Depression.

Key Takeaways

  • Long-term causes mattered most: Speculation, overproduction, unequal wealth, hire purchase debt, and unregulated banks all made the crash inevitable.
  • Black Tuesday (29 Oct 1929): Over 16 million shares were sold in panic. Share values fell from $87 billion to $30 billion in weeks.
  • Devastating consequences: Over 5,000 banks failed, unemployment hit 25%, and the crash triggered the Great Depression of the 1930s.

before.content_html:
The Scale of the Depression

The Great Depression was the worst economic crisis in American history, lasting from 1929 to the late 1930s. After the Wall Street Crash, the economy went into a devastating downward spiral. Businesses closed, banks failed, and millions lost their jobs, homes, and savings.

Many ordinary Americans who had never bought shares still lost everything. Banks had been gambling with their customers’ deposits on the stock market. When the market crashed, the banks collapsed — and innocent savers’ money went with them. There was no government insurance to protect deposits.

Unemployment and Poverty

Mass unemployment was the most devastating effect. With no welfare system, no unemployment insurance, and no safety net, losing your job meant losing everything.

The Human Cost

  • By 1933, one in four workers was unemployed. In some cities it was far worse — 80% in Toledo, Ohio and 50% in Cleveland.
  • Those who kept jobs saw wages cut by an average of 60% between 1929 and 1933.
  • 250,000 families had their homes repossessed in 1932 alone.
  • Millions went hungry. Breadlines and soup kitchens appeared in every major city, run by charities — not the government.
  • Suicide rates rose by 30% between 1929 and 1932.

Hoovervilles

Homeless Americans built makeshift shelters on waste ground, in parks, and on town edges. These shanty towns were called ‘Hoovervilles’ — a bitter, mocking reference to President Herbert Hoover, whom many blamed for the crisis.

Key Fact — Hoovervilles

Hoovervilles were built from scrap wood, tin, cardboard, and old car parts. The largest, in Central Park, New York, housed hundreds. Others appeared in Seattle, Washington D.C., St Louis, and most major cities. Bitter nicknames spread: newspapers as blankets were ‘Hoover blankets,’ empty pockets turned out were ‘Hoover flags,’ and broken cars pulled by horses were ‘Hoover wagons.’

President Hoover’s Response

Herbert Hoover was President when the Crash struck. He kept insisting recovery was near, famously declaring “Prosperity is just around the corner.” To millions of starving Americans, this showed how out of touch he was.

  • Hoover believed in ‘rugged individualism’ — the idea that Americans should help themselves, not rely on government handouts. He feared direct relief would make people dependent.
  • He encouraged voluntary action — asking businesses not to cut wages and urging charities to help the poor. This was nowhere near enough.
  • In 1931, he invested $400 million in government building projects, including the Hoover Dam, to try to create jobs. This helped, but it was too small for the scale of the crisis.
  • In 1932, he set up the Reconstruction Finance Corporation (RFC), making $1,500 million available in loans to banks and businesses. Critics called this “feeding the sparrows by feeding the horse” — it helped the rich while ordinary people starved.
  • He raised tariffs with the Hawley-Smoot Tariff (1930), which actually worsened the Depression by cutting international trade as other countries retaliated.

The Bonus Army, 1932

In summer 1932, about 20,000 World War One veterans and their families marched on Washington D.C. They demanded early payment of a war service bonus not due until 1945. These desperate, unemployed veterans set up camp near the Capitol and called themselves the Bonus Expeditionary Force (or Bonus Army).

Key Fact — The Bonus Army Incident

The Senate rejected the bonus bill, but most veterans refused to leave. Hoover ordered the US Army, led by General Douglas MacArthur, to clear the camp. Soldiers used tear gas, bayonets, and tanks to drive out the veterans and their families, burning their shelters. Two veterans were killed and over 1,000 injured, including women and children. An 11-month-old baby died in the attack. The sight of the Army attacking its own war heroes horrified the nation and destroyed Hoover’s reputation.

The Dust Bowl

While the Depression devastated cities, a separate catastrophe struck rural America. The Dust Bowl was an ecological disaster affecting the Great Plains — Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas, Colorado, and New Mexico — throughout the 1930s.

Causes of the Dust Bowl

  • Over-farming: During WWI and the 1920s, farmers ploughed up vast grasslands to plant wheat and cotton, stripping the soil’s protective covering.
  • Drought: A severe drought hit from 1931, lasting most of the decade. The exposed topsoil dried out completely.
  • Dust storms: Huge windstorms picked up loose topsoil, creating ‘black blizzards’ that travelled hundreds of miles. On ‘Black Sunday’ (14 April 1935), dust storms turned day into night.

Impact on Farmers

The Dust Bowl destroyed farming across a vast area. Crops failed, livestock died, and the land became useless. About 2.5 million people left the Dust Bowl states. Many headed to California, where they were called ‘Okies.’ They found only low-paid seasonal work and faced hostility from locals.

Key Fact — The Scale of the Dust Bowl

At its peak, the Dust Bowl affected 100 million acres. Dust storms reached as far as New York and Washington D.C., dropping Great Plains soil on politicians’ desks. The disaster showed how environmental mismanagement could worsen an economic crisis.

Impact on Different Groups

African Americans: Already the poorest group, they were hit hardest. ‘Last hired, first fired’ — Black unemployment reached 50% in many cities, double the national average. In the South, Black sharecroppers were evicted as farm income collapsed. Racial violence continued with no government help for Black communities.

Hispanic Americans: Many Mexican Americans were forced out through ‘repatriation.’ An estimated 500,000–1 million people of Mexican descent (including US citizens) were deported or pressured to leave between 1929 and 1936.

Women: Working women were accused of ‘stealing’ men’s jobs. Some states banned married women from government jobs. However, some women found work in service roles that men refused.

Children: Many were pulled out of school to work or beg. In some mining towns, 90% of children were malnourished. Thousands of teenagers became ‘hobos,’ riding freight trains looking for work.

Farmers: Falling prices, bank foreclosures, and the Dust Bowl devastated farming communities. Thousands lost farms that had been in their families for generations.

The 1932 Election

By 1932, Americans had had enough of Hoover. The Democratic candidate, Franklin D. Roosevelt (FDR), promised a “New Deal” for the American people. He pledged the “Three Rs” — Relief for the poor, Recovery for the economy, and Reform to prevent another depression.

Roosevelt won in a landslide, carrying 42 out of 48 states. Americans had rejected Hoover’s rugged individualism and voted for a president who promised the government would act. The stage was set for a dramatic change of direction.

practice_questions.marks:
All relevant and accurate points should be credited.
Top band (7-8): Complex explanation of changes. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate and detailed knowledge and understanding. Students explain complexities of change arising from differences such as time, group, social and/or economic impact.
Example: The Depression affected different groups in different ways and worsened over time. By 1933, 13 million were unemployed and wages had fallen 60%. African Americans were hit hardest — ‘last hired, first fired’ meant Black unemployment reached 50% in many cities, double the national average. Hispanic Americans faced forced ‘repatriation’ — 500,000–1 million people of Mexican descent were deported or pressured to leave. Women who worked were accused of stealing men’s jobs. Meanwhile, 250,000 families lost their homes in 1932 alone, and Hoovervilles sprang up in every major city. The Depression did not hit everyone equally — it deepened existing inequalities.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Developed explanation of changes. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate knowledge and understanding. Students consider two or more consequences with developed reasoning.

before.content_html:
FDR’s Election in 1932

Franklin Delano Roosevelt (known as FDR) won the 1932 presidential election in a landslide, defeating the unpopular Herbert Hoover. He won 42 of 48 states and 57% of the popular vote. Americans were desperate for change. Roosevelt promised a ‘New Deal’ — a bold programme of government action to tackle the Depression.

Key Fact — Roosevelt’s Promise

In his acceptance speech, Roosevelt declared: ‘I pledge you, I pledge myself, to a new deal for the American people.’ At his inauguration on 4 March 1933, he said: ‘The only thing we have to fear is fear itself.’ He projected confidence and energy — a sharp contrast with Hoover’s perceived inaction.

Roosevelt’s Approach

FDR’s approach was very different from Hoover’s. He believed the federal government had a responsibility to help ordinary Americans in crisis. He surrounded himself with the ‘Brain Trust’ — a team of expert advisors from universities and business — to design his policies. His New Deal had three main aims, known as the ‘Three Rs’:

A key idea behind the New Deal was ‘priming the pump’. If the government spent money to create jobs, those workers would spend their wages in shops and businesses, which would then hire more workers. This would create a cycle of rising prosperity. In total, the New Deal cost $50.2 billion — the biggest government spending programme in world history at the time.

The First Hundred Days (March–June 1933)

Roosevelt acted fast. In his first 100 days, he pushed 15 major pieces of legislation through Congress. He also used ‘fireside chats’ — radio broadcasts to the nation — to explain his policies in simple, reassuring language. Around 60 million Americans listened.

The Emergency Banking Act (March 1933)

Roosevelt’s first act was to declare a ‘bank holiday’ — closing all banks for four days. Government inspectors checked every bank’s accounts. Only sound banks were allowed to reopen. This restored public confidence, and within weeks Americans were depositing money back into banks instead of hiding it at home.

The Alphabet Agencies

The New Deal created many new government agencies to tackle different parts of the Depression. These became known as the ‘alphabet agencies’ because of their abbreviations:

CCC — Civilian Conservation Corps (1933): Gave work to young unemployed men aged 18–25 in conservation projects — planting trees, building roads, and preventing soil erosion. Workers received $30 per month ($25 sent home to their families). By 1942, around 3 million young men had worked in the CCC. It planted over 3 billion trees. Around 200,000 African Americans served in the CCC, but women were banned entirely.

AAA — Agricultural Adjustment Administration (1933): Aimed to raise farm prices by paying farmers to produce less. Reducing supply pushed crop prices up. Farm income doubled between 1933 and 1939. However, critics argued it was wrong to destroy food when millions were hungry. It also hurt sharecroppers and tenant farmers who were evicted when landowners took land out of production.

TVA — Tennessee Valley Authority (1933): A huge government project to develop the Tennessee Valley, one of the poorest regions in America. The TVA built 21 dams to control flooding, generate cheap hydroelectric power, and improve navigation. It brought electricity to rural areas for the first time and transformed the region’s economy. The TVA is often seen as the most successful New Deal programme.

NRA — National Recovery Administration (1933): Set minimum wages, maximum working hours, and banned child labour. Businesses that signed up displayed the ‘Blue Eagle’ symbol. However, the Supreme Court declared the NRA unconstitutional in 1935 because it gave the federal government too much power over businesses.

FERA — Federal Emergency Relief Administration (1933): Gave $500 million in grants to states for direct relief — food, clothing, and shelter. This was the first time the federal government had given money directly to help the poor.

CWA — Civil Works Administration (1933): Run by Harry Hopkins, the CWA quickly created 4 million short-term jobs for unskilled workers during the harsh winter of 1933–34 — building roads, schools, and airports. It was replaced by the WPA in 1935.

PWA — Public Works Administration (1933): Run by Harold Ickes, the PWA focused on large-scale, skilled construction projects. It spent over $6 billion building 34,000 projects, including the Triborough Bridge in New York. The PWA used skilled workers; the CWA and WPA used mostly unskilled labour. This was a key distinction.

WPA — Works Progress Administration (1935): The largest New Deal agency. Run by Harry Hopkins, the WPA employed around 8.5 million people between 1935 and 1943. It built 650,000 miles of roads, 125,000 public buildings, and 8,000 parks. It also employed artists, writers, actors, and musicians. Critics mocked some WPA jobs as ‘boondoggles’ — pointless make-work like sweeping leaves, scaring pigeons from buildings, or putting on plays. The word came from old cowboy slang for a useless task.

The Second New Deal (1935–1937)

In 1935, Roosevelt launched a second wave of New Deal laws, focusing more on long-term reform and social welfare:

The Social Security Act (1935)

This was arguably the most important and lasting New Deal reform. It created:

  • A national pension system for Americans over 65
  • Unemployment insurance — for the first time, workers who lost their jobs received temporary financial support
  • Financial help for the disabled and for mothers with dependent children

The Social Security Act created America’s first welfare state. It established the principle that the federal government had a duty to care for its citizens — a revolutionary idea in the United States.

The Wagner Act (1935)

Also known as the National Labor Relations Act, this gave workers the legal right to join trade unions and bargain collectively with employers. It set up the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) to protect workers’ rights. Union membership grew from 3.7 million in 1933 to 9 million by 1938.

Opposition to the New Deal

Despite its popularity, the New Deal faced strong opposition from several directions:

Opposition from the Right (Republicans and Big Business)

  • Republicans and business leaders accused Roosevelt of spending too much and creating dangerous federal power.
  • They called the New Deal ‘socialism’ or even ‘communism,’ saying it interfered with free enterprise and individual liberty.
  • The American Liberty League, funded by wealthy businessmen, campaigned against the New Deal.
  • Critics also attacked ‘boondoggles’ — claiming the government was paying people to do pointless jobs.

Opposition from the Left

  • Huey Long, the populist Senator from Louisiana, argued the New Deal did not go far enough. He proposed a ‘Share Our Wealth’ programme that would cap personal fortunes at $3 million and redistribute the rest to give every American family a minimum income of $5,000 per year, a free education, and a car. Long attracted millions of followers before he was assassinated in 1935.
  • Father Charles Coughlin, a Catholic priest with a radio audience of 30–40 million, initially supported FDR but turned against him. He called the New Deal too friendly to bankers and not doing enough for ordinary people.
  • Dr Francis Townsend campaigned for a pension of $200 per month for all Americans over 60, funded by a national sales tax. His plan attracted 5 million supporters.

The Supreme Court

The Supreme Court was a major threat to the New Deal. In 1935, it declared the NRA unconstitutional, and in 1936 it struck down the AAA. Conservative judges argued that New Deal agencies gave the federal government powers that belonged to individual states. In 1937, Roosevelt tried to ‘pack’ the Court by adding up to six extra, sympathetic judges. This ‘court-packing’ plan was hugely controversial and was rejected by Congress.

Key Fact — The Court-Packing Crisis

Roosevelt’s attempt to add extra judges in 1937 was his biggest political mistake. Even his supporters saw it as an attempt to undermine the courts’ independence. The plan failed, but the Supreme Court then began ruling more favourably on New Deal laws — a shift called ‘the switch in time that saved nine.’

Despite all this opposition, Roosevelt won the 1936 election in a landslide, carrying all but 2 states. He joked: ‘Everyone is against the New Deal — except the voters!’ This showed that ordinary Americans strongly supported his programmes, even if the rich and powerful did not.

Successes and Limitations of the New Deal

Jobs created: Millions were put back to work through the CCC, PWA, and WPA. Unemployment fell from 14 million (25%) in 1933 to 7 million (14%) by 1937.

Infrastructure: The New Deal built roads, bridges, dams, schools, hospitals, and airports that served America for decades. The TVA transformed an entire region.

Banking reform: The Emergency Banking Act and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) restored confidence in banks and protected savers.

Social Security: The Social Security Act (1935) created a lasting safety net — pensions, unemployment insurance, and disability support — that still exists today.

Workers’ rights: The Wagner Act strengthened trade unions and gave workers more bargaining power.

Hope and confidence: The New Deal restored hope. Roosevelt’s fireside chats and energetic leadership gave Americans confidence that their government cared.

Popular support: Roosevelt’s 1936 re-election (all but 2 states) proved the New Deal had wide public backing.

Did not end the Depression: Unemployment fell to 7 million by 1937, but when Roosevelt cut spending that year, the economy slipped back into recession (the ‘Roosevelt Recession’). Unemployment jumped back to 10 million. It was World War Two, not the New Deal, that finally ended the Depression.

African Americans: The New Deal did little for Black Americans. CCC camps were segregated. The AAA often helped white landowners at the expense of Black sharecroppers. Roosevelt refused to support anti-lynching legislation, fearing he would lose white Southern Democrats. Around 200,000 African Americans did benefit from the CCC, but discrimination was widespread.

Women: Most New Deal jobs were designed for men. Women were banned from the CCC entirely. Only around 8,000 women were enrolled in CCC-equivalent programmes, compared to 3 million men. Some NRA codes set lower wages for women than for men.

Huge government debt: The New Deal cost $50.2 billion in total — the biggest government scheme in world history. Critics said this was unsustainable.

Did not fix the economic system: American capitalism stayed the same. Wealth inequality persisted, and the root causes of the Depression were not fully addressed.

States’ Rights vs Federal Government

The New Deal permanently changed the relationship between the federal government and the American people. Before Roosevelt, most Americans expected state governments — not Washington — to handle welfare, jobs, and economic problems. The New Deal shifted power to the federal government on a scale never seen before. This was a revolutionary change. From this point on, Americans looked to the president and Congress to solve national crises. The debate over states’ rights versus federal power remains one of the biggest issues in American politics today.

before.content_html:
1930s Popular Culture

Before looking at the war, it is important to understand American culture during the 1930s Depression. Despite widespread poverty, popular culture boomed — much of it was escapism, helping people forget their troubles.

Jazz remained hugely popular. Big band swing music filled dance halls across the country. In cinema, ‘talkies’ (films with sound) had replaced silent films from 1928 onwards. Hollywood produced musicals, comedies, and adventure films that drew huge audiences. By the end of the 1930s, the first colour films appeared, including The Wizard of Oz (1939). Comic books also emerged in this period — Superman first appeared in 1938. Radio remained the main source of home entertainment, with comedy shows, dramas, and music reaching millions. All of this culture gave Americans a way to escape the misery of the Depression, even if only for a few hours.

From Neutrality to War

When war broke out in Europe in September 1939, most Americans wanted to stay out of it. However, Roosevelt gradually moved the USA towards supporting the Allies.

In November 1939, Roosevelt introduced the Cash and Carry Plan. This allowed Britain and France to buy American weapons, as long as they paid cash and carried the goods in their own ships. It was an important stepping stone between neutrality and full involvement. Roosevelt also gave Britain 50 old warships in exchange for the right to use British military bases — another step closer to war.

Pearl Harbor

The United States entered World War Two on 7 December 1941, after Japan’s surprise attack on the US naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. The attack killed over 2,400 Americans and destroyed much of the Pacific fleet. President Roosevelt called it ‘a date which will live in infamy’ and Congress declared war the next day.

The war ended the Great Depression, reshaped the role of women and African Americans, and turned the USA into the world’s leading superpower.

Economic Recovery Through War Production

After a decade of Depression, wartime production created a huge economic boom. Factories that had stood idle were now running around the clock, producing weapons, vehicles, ships, and aircraft.

Even before Pearl Harbor, the war economy was already working. By 1941, unemployment had fallen to 5 million as factories geared up to supply the Allies. The US government spent over $300 billion on the war effort between 1941 and 1945 — far more than anything the New Deal had attempted. This finally achieved full employment.

The War Production Miracle

American factories switched to war materials at astonishing speed. The Ford Willow Run plant in Michigan went from making cars to building B-24 Liberator bombers — at its peak, one every 63 minutes. Shipbuilder Henry J. Kaiser cut Liberty Ship construction time from 230 days to just 42 days.

By 1945, American factories had produced 300,000 aircraft, 86,000 tanks, 2.5 million trucks, and 6,500 naval vessels.

Cash and Carry, Lend-Lease, and Global Dominance

The Cash and Carry Plan (1939) was followed by the Lend-Lease Act, signed on 11 March 1941. Lend-Lease let the USA supply weapons, food, oil, and equipment to Britain, the Soviet Union, China, and other Allies without requiring immediate payment.

Lend-Lease totalled $50.1 billion (over $700 billion today). Britain received $31.4 billion; the Soviet Union received $11.3 billion. These programmes kept the Allies fighting and boosted the American economy — factories producing Lend-Lease goods employed millions of workers.

By 1945, the USA held two-thirds of the world’s gold reserves and produced half of the world’s manufactured goods. Average wages rose by 44% during the war. Personal savings jumped from $6.3 billion (1940) to $37 billion (1945).

The Experience of African Americans During WWII

World War Two was a turning point for African Americans. The war created new jobs, challenged racial attitudes, and planted the seeds of the civil rights movement. However, segregation and discrimination continued throughout the war.

The Double V Campaign

In February 1942, the Pittsburgh Courier — a leading Black newspaper — launched the ‘Double V’ campaign. The two ‘V’s stood for victory abroad (against fascism) and victory at home (against racial discrimination). The campaign highlighted the contradiction of fighting for freedom overseas while Black Americans were denied basic rights at home.

The Double V campaign gained huge support. It helped politicise African Americans and raised awareness of racial injustice among the wider public.

A. Philip Randolph and Executive Order 8802

A. Philip Randolph, head of the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters (a Black trade union), threatened to organise a March on Washington of 100,000 African Americans in January 1941 to protest racial discrimination in defence industries.

To prevent the march, Roosevelt issued Executive Order 8802 on 25 June 1941 — the first federal order banning racial discrimination since Reconstruction. It banned discrimination in defence industries and set up the Fair Employment Practices Committee (FEPC).

Key Fact — Executive Order 8802

This was the first presidential executive order on race since the Civil War era. African Americans in defence industries rose from 3% (1942) to 8% (1945). Over one million Black workers gained factory jobs. However, African Americans were typically paid half of what white workers earned for the same roles. The FEPC had limited enforcement powers — it could investigate but not force employers to comply.

African Americans in the Military

Over one million African Americans served in the US military during WWII. The armed forces remained strictly segregated — Black soldiers served in separate units, often under white officers, and were frequently given non-combat roles like loading cargo.

Despite this, some Black units won distinction. The Tuskegee Airmen — the first African American fighter pilots — flew over 15,000 missions. The 761st Tank Battalion fought in the Battle of the Bulge and earned a Presidential Unit Citation. These achievements undermined racist claims that Black soldiers were inferior.

The Great Migration Accelerates

The war sped up the Great Migration of African Americans from the rural South to northern and western cities. Between 1940 and 1945, about 1.5 million Black Americans moved to cities like Detroit, Chicago, Los Angeles, and Pittsburgh for factory work.

This brought new opportunities but also tension. In June 1943, a race riot in Detroit lasted three days and left 34 people dead (25 of them African American). White workers often resented Black newcomers competing for jobs and housing.

The Experience of Women During WWII

With 16 million men in the armed forces, women were urgently needed to fill their jobs. The scale of female employment was unprecedented.

‘Rosie the Riveter’

The government launched a propaganda campaign to recruit women. The iconic ‘Rosie the Riveter’ — a strong woman in overalls flexing her bicep with the slogan ‘We Can Do It!’ — became the symbol of women’s wartime contribution.

Key Fact — Women in the Workforce

Working women rose from 12 million (1940) to 18 million (1945). By 1944, women made up 37% of the workforce. Over 300,000 women served in military roles such as the Women’s Army Corps (WAC) and WAVES. The WASPs (Women Airforce Service Pilots) were trained to deliver aircraft to war zones, freeing up male pilots for combat. Women worked as welders, riveters, electricians, and crane operators — jobs previously seen as impossible for women.

Limitations for Women

Women still faced real inequality. They earned only 65% of what men earned for the same work. Childcare was a major problem — the government funded some day nurseries, but provision was poor. Women were expected to go back to domestic roles once the war ended.

After 1945, 4 million women left the workforce to make way for returning soldiers. Surveys showed 75% of wartime women workers wanted to keep their jobs. The experience of wartime work changed women’s expectations permanently and laid the groundwork for the later feminist movement.

Japanese American Internment

One of the darkest episodes of the war was the forced internment of Japanese Americans. After Pearl Harbor, anti-Japanese hysteria swept the country. In February 1942, Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066, authorising the removal of all people of Japanese ancestry from the West Coast.

About 120,000 Japanese Americans — two-thirds of them US citizens — were forced into ten remote internment camps. Families had only days to sell their homes and possessions, often for a fraction of their value. They lost an estimated $400 million in property.

Camps were surrounded by barbed wire and armed guards. Families lived in cramped barracks with shared facilities. Despite this, internees organised schools, newspapers, and community activities.

No Japanese American was ever found guilty of spying or sabotage. The internment was driven by racial prejudice, wartime hysteria, and economic jealousy. Japanese Americans in Hawaii were not interned, even though they made up a third of the population there.

In 1988, President Reagan signed the Civil Liberties Act, formally apologising and awarding $20,000 to each surviving internee.

The GI Bill (1944)

The GI Bill (officially the Servicemen’s Readjustment Act), signed on 22 June 1944, helped 16 million returning veterans readjust to civilian life. It provided:

  • College or vocational education — the government paid tuition and a living allowance. By 1956, nearly 8 million veterans had used this.
  • Low-cost home loans — no deposit required, fuelling the post-war suburban boom.
  • Unemployment insurance — $20 per week for up to a year (nicknamed the ‘52-20 Club’).

The GI Bill is often credited with creating the American middle class. However, many African American veterans could not benefit equally — racist banks denied them home loans, and white universities (especially in the South) refused to admit them.
before.conclusion_html:
Conclusion

World War Two transformed the United States. Massive government spending ended the Depression, and America emerged as the world’s dominant superpower. Millions of women entered the workforce, and African Americans gained new jobs while challenging segregation. Yet deep contradictions remained: Japanese Americans were interned, the military stayed segregated, African Americans were paid half of white wages, and women were pushed back into domestic roles after 1945. The rising expectations the war created would shape the decades that followed.

Key Takeaways

  • Economic transformation: Cash and Carry (1939) and Lend-Lease ($50.1 billion) supported the Allies and boosted American industry. Unemployment dropped from 14.6% to 1.2%. The USA emerged holding two-thirds of the world’s gold reserves.
  • Seeds of civil rights: The Double V campaign, Executive Order 8802, and over one million Black soldiers’ service challenged discrimination — but African Americans still faced segregation and were paid half of white wages.
  • Women’s changing role: Six million women entered the workforce. WASPs delivered aircraft to war zones. Although most women were pushed out after 1945, their experience changed expectations permanently.

before.content_html:
The Post-War Economic Boom

After World War Two ended in 1945, the United States entered a period of huge economic growth. Unlike the fragile boom of the 1920s, this one was sustained and widespread. The USA emerged as the world’s dominant economic and military superpower. Many Americans felt they were living the American Dream — the idea that through hard work, anyone could achieve prosperity and success.

Why Did the Economy Boom?

  • Wartime production: Factories switched from making tanks and aircraft to cars, fridges, and televisions. They were modern, efficient, and ready to meet demand.
  • Pent-up demand: Consumer goods had been rationed during the war. Americans had saved around $140 billion and were eager to spend.
  • Government spending: Cold War defence spending kept factories busy. The Korean War (1951) was another boost — military spending accounted for around 10% of GDP in the 1950s.
  • New technology: Wartime innovations were adapted for peacetime. Televisions, synthetic materials, jet travel, and plastics created new industries.
  • Population growth: The ‘baby boom’ (see below) created huge demand for housing, schools, and consumer goods.

Truman’s ‘Fair Deal’

After Roosevelt’s death in 1945, President Harry Truman promised Americans a ‘Fair Deal.’ He said: ‘Every segment of our population has a right to expect from his government a fair deal.’ Truman’s policies continued the New Deal approach — using government spending to support jobs, housing, and welfare. President Eisenhower (1953–1961) continued many of these programmes too. The idea that government should help ordinary people was now firmly established.

The GI Bill

The Servicemen’s Readjustment Act of 1944 (the GI Bill) was one of the most important laws in American history. It gave returning veterans:

  • Education: The government paid tuition and living costs. By 1947, veterans were 49% of all college admissions. Nearly 8 million veterans used this benefit.
  • Home loans: Low-interest, zero-deposit mortgages helped millions buy homes, driving suburban growth.
  • Unemployment support: $20 per week for up to a year while veterans found work.
Key Fact — The GI Bill’s Impact

The GI Bill opened higher education to millions of working-class Americans, creating a larger, more skilled workforce. Before WWII, college was mainly for the wealthy. However, Black veterans often struggled to access benefits — many colleges (especially in the South) refused to admit them, and banks sometimes refused mortgages to Black applicants in white areas.

The Baby Boom

When soldiers returned home, the birth rate soared. Between 1946 and 1964, about 76 million babies were born — the ‘baby boomers.’ The peak year was 1957, with 4.3 million births.

The baby boom created huge demand for housing, schools, children’s products, and food. It fuelled suburban growth as families needed bigger homes. In the 1960s and 1970s, the baby boomers themselves became a powerful cultural and political force.

Suburbia and Levittown

One of the most visible changes was the rapid growth of suburbs — residential communities on the outskirts of cities. They offered affordable homes, gardens, good schools, and a quieter life away from crowded inner cities.

Levittown

The most famous suburb was Levittown, built by William Levitt on Long Island, New York, from 1947. Levitt used assembly-line techniques — each identical house could be built in just 16 minutes per stage. Houses started at $7,990 (about $100,000 today). Levittown eventually held 17,000 homes and 82,000 people.

Key Fact — Suburban Growth

By 1960, one-third of all Americans lived in suburbs. Suburban population grew by 47% in the 1950s. However, the suburbs were overwhelmingly white. Levittown’s contracts explicitly banned sales to African Americans. This practice, known as ‘redlining,’ trapped Black families in overcrowded inner-city areas with declining services.

Suburban Women’s Isolation

Suburban life was not perfect for everyone. Many women who had worked during the war were now expected to be full-time housewives. Isolated in their suburban homes, unable to work, some women felt bored, lonely, and depressed. This sense of frustration would later inspire Betty Friedan’s feminist movement in the 1960s.

Consumer Culture

Post-war America saw a consumer explosion that dwarfed even the 1920s:

Television

Television was the defining technology of the era. In 1945, fewer than 10,000 homes had a TV. By 1960, 46 million did — about 90% of all homes. TV transformed entertainment, news, advertising, and politics. Adverts beamed into living rooms drove consumer spending.

Car Culture

The car became central to American life. By the mid-1950s, there were over 60 million cars. The Interstate Highway Act of 1956, signed by President Eisenhower, built 41,000 miles of interstate highways — the largest public works project in American history. Highways made suburban living practical and spawned new businesses: drive-in cinemas, drive-in restaurants (including the first McDonald’s in 1955), shopping malls, and motels.

Consumer Goods and Credit

Advertising, hire purchase (buying on credit), and rising incomes meant Americans bought more than ever. Hire purchase increased by 800% between 1945 and 1957. By the late 1950s, the average family owned a car, television, washing machine, and refrigerator. America consumed one-third of the world’s goods despite having only 6% of the world’s population.

Rock and Roll

Rock and roll was the biggest cultural change of the 1950s. It grew out of African American rhythm and blues music and became hugely popular with white teenagers.

Elvis Presley — the ‘King of Rock and Roll’ — became a sensation with hits like Hound Dog and Jailhouse Rock. Other stars included Chuck Berry, who helped define the rock and roll guitar sound, and Buddy Holly. Their music thrilled young people and horrified many adults.

Rock and roll created a ‘generation gap’ between teenagers and their parents. Adults criticised the music for encouraging rebellion, sexual freedom, and disrespect for authority. For the first time, teenagers emerged as a distinct group with their own money, music, fashion, and identity. Businesses quickly targeted this new market. The teenager became a powerful consumer.

The Limits of Post-War Prosperity

African Americans: Black Americans still faced segregation, especially in the South. They were excluded from many suburbs, faced job discrimination, and lived in poverty at much higher rates. In 1950, average Black family income was 54% of white family income.

Inner-city poverty: As white families moved to suburbs (‘white flight’), inner cities lost tax revenue, jobs, and services. The remaining population — mainly Black and Hispanic — faced declining schools, rising crime, and crumbling infrastructure.

Rural poverty: In areas like Appalachia and the Deep South, millions lived in severe poverty without proper healthcare, education, or housing.

Conformity and discontent: Suburban life was criticised for its conformity and materialism. Writers like Jack Kerouac (the Beat Generation) questioned whether the ‘American Dream’ was truly fulfilling or just shallow consumerism.

• rock and roll and the emergence of teenage culture
• the post-war economic boom and rising living standards?
